title: Swallowing Our Pride and Turning to the Experts
author: Golazeski, Daniel
summary: Daniel Golazeski makes the case for end-of-year student evaluations of teachers -- a practice rarely required but consistently the most meaningful professional feedback a teacher can receive. His central argument: students who have observed 150+ lessons and spent thousands of minutes in a classroom are the world's foremost experts on whether that teacher is effective, and the fear of honest student feedback is precisely what keeps most teachers from seeking it. The article provides a five-step guide to creating meaningful evaluations: building on existing examples; tailoring questions to your own teaching; writing items from the student's perspective ('Mr. G cares about me'); keeping responses anonymous; and grading for completion, not positivity. Golazeski identifies the single most diagnostic question a teacher can ask: 'If I had the option, I would choose [teacher's name] to teach one of my classes next year' -- simultaneously an accountability measure and a year-round teaching goal. He also offers a graceful on-ramp for teachers not ready to receive feedback this year: write the evaluation now, use it as a target from September forward, and give yourself a 365-day head start on the questions students will eventually answer.
points: Students who have observed 150+ lessons are the world's foremost experts on whether their teacher is effective -- their feedback is more diagnostic than any administrative observation rubric, and most teachers never access it.

The single most powerful evaluation question is whether students would voluntarily choose that teacher again -- it simultaneously functions as an accountability measure and a concrete teaching goal that can drive an entire year's instruction.

Writing evaluation items from the student's perspective ('Mr. G cares about me') rather than the teacher's ('Teacher demonstrates care') produces more honest and usable responses by eliminating bureaucratic distancing.

Anonymity is non-negotiable: if students believe responses will affect their grades, none of the feedback is reliable -- grading for completion, not content, removes the incentive to perform satisfaction rather than report truth.

Teachers not ready to receive evaluations this June should write the evaluation now and use it as a teaching target for next year -- the 365-day head start turns the questionnaire into a prospective lesson plan for the entire year.
quotes: The best way to know if someone is a good teacher is to sit in their room and watch them teach... That's what makes evaluations from our students so valuable. They saw us teach over one-hundred-and-fifty lessons. They spent thousands of minutes in our classrooms. They are the foremost experts on whether or not we are good teachers.

The fear of getting brutally honest feedback from the people who have spent more time in our classroom than anyone else can be paralyzing. But cutting ourselves off from this feedback denies us the most meaningful critiques we could ever receive.

Every year that I asked students to complete an end-of-year evaluation, I got at least some feedback that genuinely hurt. This was far from fun, but nothing improved my craft more than being willing to accept honest critiques from my students.

If you can't give out an evaluation this June, then prepare one to give out next June. This gives you a three-hundred-and-sixty-five-day head start. Knowing what questions your students will answer next June can guide your teaching next September through May.

Instead of 'Teacher cares about the well-being of students,' I used, 'Mr. G cares about me and my well-being.' Instead of 'Teacher presents the subject matter in a way that makes sense,' I used, 'I am able to understand the lesson when Mr. G is teaching the class.'

Do you agree with the following statement? 'If I had the option, I would choose (insert teacher's name) to teach one of my classes next year.' This one question can tell us more about our teaching than a five-page teacher observation rubric.
The answer is sitting in front of us each June. We just need to be willing to ask.
